subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Café Procope: The Oldest Café in Paris
description: A fast breakdown of Café Procope: The Oldest Café in Paris for builders.

hook.text: Le Procope opened in 1686 and is still serving today—making it the oldest continuously operating café in Paris.

buildup.text: Sicilian immigrant Francesco Procopio dei Coltelli opened it across from the Comédie-Française theater.

discovery.text: Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot, and Benjamin Franklin all drank here. The Encyclopédie was partly planned at its tables.

twist.text: During the French Revolution, it became a meeting place for revolutionaries. Marat and Danton plotted there.

climax.text: A single café witnessed the Enlightenment, the Revolution, and the birth of the Encyclopédie—spanning centuries of change.

punchline.text: Still open since 1686. The café outlasted empires and revolutions.

quiz.question: What makes Le Procope historically significant?
options: It's the biggest café in Paris
Voltaire, Rousseau, and revolutionaries frequented it since 1686

details.summary: Le Procope, opened in 1686 by Sicilian Francesco Procopio dei Coltelli, claims to be the oldest continuously operating cafe in Paris. Voltaire, Rousseau, and Diderot all frequented it. Benjamin Franklin and later the French revolutionaries plotted there. It bridges three centuries of French history.
details.whyItMatters: Le Procope connects the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and modern cafe culture in a single location. It shows the enduring power of gathering spaces.
takeaways: Le Procope opened in 1686 and still operates today
Voltaire, Rousseau, and Franklin were among its patrons

faq.question: Is Le Procope really the oldest cafe in Paris?
faq.answer: It is the oldest continuously operating establishment in Paris originally founded as a cafe. It has changed formats over the centuries, operating now as a restaurant-cafe. Some dispute whether continuity counts when the format changed, but its founding date of 1686 is well documented.

faq.question: What role did Le Procope play in the French Revolution?
faq.answer: Revolutionaries including Danton, Marat, and Robespierre met there to discuss strategy. Its proximity to the Comedie Francaise attracted politically engaged audiences. Legend says the young Napoleon left his hat as collateral when he could not pay his bill.
